INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
This amicus curiae brief is submitted by the National Education Association (“NEA”).1 NEA is the nation’s largest professional association and union, representing nearly three million members. The vast majority of NEA’s members serve as teachers, counselors,
and education support professionals in our nation’s
public schools. NEA’s mission is to advocate for education professionals and work with communities to fulfill
the promise of public education to prepare every student to succeed in a diverse and interdependent world.
NEA has a strong interest in this case, which presents a question about the circumstances in which individual parents may enlist the federal courts in disrupting or diverting the provision of important public
services—including the education of the Nation’s
youth in our public schools—to accommodate the parents’ personal preferences.
NEA believes that educating young people is a
partnership between administrators, teachers, students, and their families. NEA knows that the involvement of parents and caregivers is critical to the education and growth of children: when families are involved, students attend school more regularly, stay in
school longer, and perform at higher levels. NEA also
recognizes that in a diverse nation, absolute consensus
in public policy about services for children is rare, and
people who care about children may have reasonable

1 Amicus states that no party’s counsel authored the brief in
whole or in part; no party’s counsel contributed money that was
intended to fund preparing or submitting the brief; and no person—other than NEA, its members, or its counsel —contributed
money tha t was intended to fund preparing or submitting the
brief. See Sup. Ct. R. 37.6.

2
disagreements. In a healthy democracy, it is the job of
democratically elected and properly appointed decisionmakers to develop and implement policy solutions
to difficult problems.
NEA submits this brief in support of Respondents
to elucidate the troubling consequences that a ruling
in favor of Petitioners would have on public programming that serves children.  The judgment of the Ninth
Circuit is correct and should be affirmed  or, alternatively, the writ of certiorari should be dismissed as improvidently granted.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
In pursuit of a challenge to a set of Washington
State laws that have no current or certainly impending
effect on them or their children, Petitioners urge this
Court to adopt a new theory of standing to sidestep
what have long been understood as the irredu cible
minimum requirements of Article III  of the U.S. Constitution. Amicus NEA urges the Court to reject Petitioners’ attempt to refashion the law of standing in this
way.
One of the primary functions of this Court’s standing jurisprudence is to prevent federal courts from adjudicating generalized grievances that transform lifetime judicial appointees into unelected and unrepresentative policymakers. Indeed, Article III extends the
federal courts’ purview to “cases” and “controversies,”
not to all matters of public concern. To ensure that the
federal judiciary maintains its properly limited role,
this Court’s cases establish that in any case before a
federal court the plaintiff must show (i) that he suffered an injury in fact that is concrete, particularized,
and actual or imminent; (ii) that the injury was likely

3
caused by the defendant; and (iii) that the injury would
likely be redressed by judicial relief.
Petitioners’ new theory of standing replaces these
requirements with a single nebulous inquiry into
whether a plaintiff is an “object” of the challenged law
or policy. Under this approach, it is apparently of no
moment that a plaintiff ha s suffered no actual or imminent injury, that its claimed injuries are entirely
subjective or self -inflicted, or that any harm would
only come about as the result of a speculative or attenuated chain of events. Nor does this novel theory contain any  limiting principle that constrains a court’s
standing inquiry. Instead, it opens the door to the adjudication of generalized grievances in federal court.
Adopting Petitioners’ open-ended theory of standing theory is especially concerning because it would
burden important governmental services —and especially K -12 public education —with unworkable demands. Public institutions and decisionmakers will be
pulled in every direction at once, forced to determine
how to develop program s that are consistent with
every parenting style and preference.
This would be particularly true for K -12 public
schools, given Petitioners’ expansive view of standing
and misguided conception of the scope of parental
rights protected by the Constitution. Under Petitioners’ approach, i ndividual disagreements with any  aspect of the broad array of programming, services, and
instruction provided by public schools would be open
to constitutional challenge—not just by parents of students in the school, but by anyone who theoretically
could become a parent of a student in the school. This
would place untenable burdens on schools and teachers. And it would contravene this Court’s longstanding
recognition that federal courts are poorly equipped to

4
second-guess the day- to-day operations of K-12
schools.
Amicus NEA therefore submits this brief to emphasize the negative impacts that adopting this theory
of standing would have on public programming that
serves children and families, including schools.
ARGUMENT
A. A fundamental purpose of this Court’s
standing jurisprudence is to prevent the
adjudication of generalized grievances
that improperly allow Article III judges to
act as unelected policymakers
“The Constitution confers limited authority on
each branch of the Federal Government.” Spokeo, Inc.
v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330, 337 (2016) . For the federal
courts, Article III  limits them to exercising the “judicial power” to decide “cases” and “controversies.” And
such cases or controversies “exist only if a plaintiff has
standing to sue.” United States v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670,
675 (2023). The requirement for standing is therefore
“founded in concern about the proper —and properly
limited—role of the courts in a democratic society.”
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490, 498 (1975).
One of the primary purposes of this Court’s standing doctrine is to prevent the adjudication of a plaintiff’s “generalized” grievance that asserts only an “interest in proper application of the Constitution and
laws.” Hollingsworth v. Perry , 570 U.S. 693, 706
(2013). This is “an essential limit” on the judicial
power, ensuring that lifetime appointees to the federal
bench act “as judges, and do not engage in policymaking properly left to elected representatives.” Id. at 700
(emphasis omitted);  see also Lance v. Coffman , 549
U.S. 437, 439 (2007)  (per curiam) (“[This Court’s]

5
refusal to serve as a forum for generalized g rievances
has a lengthy pedigree.”).
Under the standing doctrine’s prohibition on entertaining generalized grievances, federal courts have
no “roving commission to publicly opine on every legal
question” or authority to “issue advisory opinions.”
TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez , 594 U.S. 413, 423 –24
(2021); see also Hein v. Freedom From Religion Found.,
Inc., 551 U.S. 587, 593 (2007) (explaining that, absent
such a limitation, “the federal courts would cease to
function as courts of law and would be cast in the role
of general complaint bureaus”). Likewise, would-be litigants have no ability to “sue merely because their legal objection is accompanied by a strong moral, ideological, or policy objection to a government action.”
Food & Drug Admin. v. All. for Hippocratic Med., 602
U.S. 367, 381 (2024) . Instead, a plaintiff must show
from the outset of t he litigation and at every stage
thereafter that the “legal questions presented to the
court will be resolved . . . in a concrete factual context
conducive to a realistic appreciation of the consequences of judicial action.” Diamond Alternative Energy, LLC v. EPA, 606 U.S. 100, 111 (2025)  (citation
omitted).
To establish such a case or controversy for purposes of Article III standing, a plaintiff must show: “(i)
that he suffered an injury in fact that is concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent; (ii) that the injury
was likely caused by the defendant; and (iii) that the
injury would likely be redressed by judicial relief.”
TransUnion, 594 U.S. at 423. These elements “distinguish cases and controversies fit for judicial resolution
from questions of public policy reserved to the elected
branches or abstract disputes better left to the debating hall.” First Choice Women’s Res. Ctrs., Inc. v. Davenport, 608 U.S. 174, 183 (2026) . And because these

6
three elements comprise “the irreducible constit utional minimum of standing,” they dictate the standard that Petitioners must be held to —and that they
ultimately fail to meet —here. Diamond Alternative
Energy, 606 U.S. at 111 (citation omitted).
B. Petitioners’ novel and expansive standing
theories fail every limitation in this
Court’s caselaw guarding against the adjudication of generalized grievances
Petitioners seek to challenge a Washington State
statute that regulates licensed yout h shelters. See
Wash. Rev. Code § 13.32A.082. Usually, when a runaway youth arrives at a licensed shelter, the shelter
contacts the youth’s parents within 72 hours. Id.
§ 13.32A.082(1)(b)(i). If, however, the runaway youth
is seeking or receiving protected healthcare services—
such as pregnancy or gender affirming care —the law
requires the shelter to notify the Department  of Children, Youth, and Families , which then contacts the
youth’s parents and refers the youth to voluntary behavioral health and family reconciliation services. Id.
§ 13.32A.082(3).
However, Petitioners have no children who ar e—
or ever have been —in a licensed shelter and have
never been offered the referrals to services that they
find objectionable. Their primary argument before this
Court, therefore, is that they may dispense with ordinary standing requirements and instead avail themselves of what they call “object-of-the-law standing” to
mount their challenge.  Pet. Br. 30 . Per Petitioners,
this supposed form of standing  sidesteps any need to
establish the traditional elements of injury, causation,

7
and redressability.2 See id. at 21–31. But as the State
shows conclusively in its brief, Petitioners’ novel “object-of-the-law” theory reflects a basic misreading of
this Court’s precedent, see Resp. Br. 26 –28, and it
would make a hash of existing caselaw if this Court
were to accept it, id. at 28–29. Indeed, Petitioners’ theory is so misguided and unworkable that some of their
own most prominent supporting amici disavow it.3 See
Am. First Legal Found. Amicus Br.  25 (“More importantly, an “object” of a challenged policy (whatever

2 T he State points out  that Petitioners did not raise their
novel “object-of-the-law standing” argument below. See Resp. Br.
23. Where a plaintiff has “raised for the first time a novel alternative theory of standing,” this Court should follow its existing
practice of “declin[ing] to consider” the newly raised argument.
California v. Texas, 593 U.S. 659, 674 (2021). Indeed, it would be
appropriate for this Court to dismiss the writ of certiorari as improvidently granted, as the State suggests in its brief. See Resp.
Br. 20–24.
3 Even setting aside the larger deficiencies in Petitioners’
“object-of-the-law” theory of standing, their challenge to one provision of Washington law fails the requirements of Article III  for
other reasons. Specifically, Petitioners seek to challenge the constitutionality of Wash. Rev. Code §  71.34.530, a provision of
Washington law that does not regulate licensed homeless shelters, but instead generally allows adolescents thirteen and older
to “request and receive outpatient [behavioral health] treatment
without the consent of the adolescent’s parent.” See Pet. Br. 30,
44–45. Yet, nowhere in their brief or in the pleadings below do
Petitioners actually identify a named defendant with the authority to enforce or administer the challenged statute. As a result,
Petitioners cannot establish the redressability element of standing required for their challenge. After all, in the absence of a
named defendant with authority to enforce or administer the
challenged statute, even a judgment in Petitioners’ favor on the
merits would not give them “legally enforceable protection” from
any supposed harm caused by the law. Haaland v. Brackeen, 599
U.S. 255, 293 (2023); see also California, 593 U.S. at 672 (explaining that remedies “operate with r espect to specific parties” and
not “on legal rules in the abstract”) (citation omitted).

8
that means) is not excused from his obligation to plead
and prove the components of Article III  standing—injury in fact, traceability, and redressability.”); see also
U.S. Amicus Br. 13, 23 (reiterating the longstanding
elements of standing and dismissing Petitioners’ approach as “too broad”).
Although there are many features of Petitioners’
theory that warrant scrutiny, Amicus NEA’s primary
concern is the risk that what masquerades as a theory
of standing is, in reality, an open door to adjudicating
generalized grievances in the federal courts . Accordingly, we emphasize several ways in which Petitioners’
novel theory disregards the most crucial aspects of the
standing inquiry that prevent federal- court jurisdiction from encroaching on the other organs of our democracy.
The requirement for a present or imminent
injury. This Court has consistently held that speculative “allegations of possible future injury are not sufficient” to support standing. Clapper v. Amnesty Int ’l
USA, 568 U.S. 398, 409 (2013)  (citation omitted). Instead, Article III  demands that a plaintiff’s asserted
injury must be actually occurring or “certainly impending” Ibid.; see also All. for Hippocratic Med. , 602
U.S. at 381 (explaining that “the injury must be actual
or imminent, not speculative —meaning that the injury must have already occurred or be likely to occur
soon”). This requirement is a first line of defense for
identifying and filtering out generalized grievances; it
ensures that the court is addressing a genuine dispute
rather than operating as a “a legislative assembly, a
town square, or a faculty lounge.” All. for Hippocratic
Med., 602 U.S. at 382.
By contrast, Petitioners’ claims rely substantially
on predictions of injury that may occur, if at all, at
some unknown point in the future. See, e.g., Pet. Br.

9
17 (claiming as a sufficient injury that one of Petitioners’ children could at some point “run away to get the
treatment their parents reject”). Allowing a ny parent
to sue on the theory that they are an “object” of a law
by virtue of the fact that they have children —while
having no actual or certainly impending injury —
would fatally undermine the longstanding prohibition
on generalized grievances.
Declining standing based on asserted harms
that are subjective, manufactured, or self -inflicted. This Court has consistently rejected claims of
standing based on  the notion that the mere presence
of a law “on the books” will cause a plaintiff to “feel
inhibited” in his actions. Younger v. Harris, 401 U. S.
37, 42 (1971); see also Laird v. Tatum, 408 U.S. 1, 13–
14 (1972) (“Allegations of a subjective ‘chill’ are not an
adequate substitute for a claim of specific present objective harm or a threat of specific future harm”). Under this principle, a plaintiff “cannot manufacture
standing merely by inflicting harm on themselves
based on their fears of hypothetical future harm.”
Murthy v. Missouri , 603 U.S. 43, 73 (2024)  (citation
omitted); see also Los Angeles v. Lyons , 461 U.S. 95,
107 n.8 (1983) (explaining that what matters for purposes of standing is the “ reality of the threat of . . .
injury,” not “subjective apprehensions”)  (emphasis
omitted).
By contrast, the only present (as opposed to future)
harm Petitioners attempt to identify is that the existence of Washington’s laws on the books gives them
“fear” and causes them to “chill their speech at home
and change their parenting strategy.” Pet. Br. 43. But
allowing standing on subjective grounds that could be
invoked by nearly anyone means that “the federal
courts would be open to virtually any citizen who

10
desired an advisory opinion.” Ellis v. Dyson, 421 U.S.
426, 446 n.12 (1975) (Powell, J., dissenting).
Rejecting standing based on speculati on or
attenuated claims of causation. This Court has
consistently rejected claims of standing where the elements of causation an d redressability are based on a
“highly attenuated chain of possibilities.” Clapper, 568
U.S. at 410–11. And this is especially true where links
in the causal chain include speculation about the independent action of others . See Simon v. Eastern Ky.
Welfare Rts. Org., 426 U.S. 26, 41 –42 (1976); see also
All. for Hippocratic Med ., 602 U.S. at 383 . Without
such a limitation, a generalized grievance could become a federal court judgment through “an ingenious
academic exercise in the conceivable.” United States v.
Students Challenging Regul. Agency Procs ., 412 U.S.
669, 688 (1973).
By contrast, the chain that would connect Petitioners to any conceivable injury is both highly speculative
and depends on a chain of events that could at any
point be disrupted. As the Ninth Circuit recognized below, before any parent suffers an injury on account of
the challenged Washington laws, their child would
have to:
(1) have a gender identity different from their
sex assigned at birth; (2) be seeking gender-affirming care; (3) run away; (4) find a licensed
shelter; (5) decline to share parental information with the Department; (6) accept the
Department’s referral for behavioral health
services; and (7) obtain mental health care
from a provider without parental consent
based on the Department’s referral. (Resp. Br.
42)

11
This potential chain of events becomes even more
speculative and attenuated because other actors—including Petitioners’ own children —could easily break
a link of the chain that  that connects Petitioners’ asserted harms to the actions of the State. After all, as
Petitioners themselves admit, “virtually all youth already seek to circumvent their parents’ authority and
desires without needing any legal encouragement.”
Pet. Br. 41. This is far from the “high degree of immediacy” that would be needed “to reduce of the possibility of deci ding a case in which no injury would have
occurred at all.” Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife , 504 U.S.
555, 565 n.2 (1992).
Rejecting theories of standing that lack any
meaningful limiting principle. This Court has consistently rejected theories of standing that are “boundless,” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc ., 568 U.S. 85, 99
(2013), or lack “any meaningful limiting principles,”
Whole Woman ’s Health v. Jackson , 595 U.S. 30, 40
(2021); see also Valley Forge Christian Coll. v. Americans United for Separation of Church & State, Inc., 454
U.S. 464, 489 (1982) (rejecting a plaintiff’s standing argument because there was “no principled basis for confining” it); Murthy, 603 U.S. at 75  (same with regard
to a plaintiff’s “startlingly broad” theory of standing).
The reason for this is obvio us: if this Court were to
start down the path of accepting such a theory, it may
“not end until virtually every citizen had standing to
challenge virtually every government action that they
do not like —an approach to standing that this Court
has consistently rejected as flatly inconsistent with Article III.” All. for Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S. at 392.
By contrast, Petitioners identify no coherent principle that would limit their expansive “object -of-thelaw” theory of standing. For example, Petitioners suggest that one limiting principle of their theory for this

12
case is that it would extend only to parents in Washington State. See Pet. Br. 29–31. But such a limitation
makes little sense if the relevant harms, as Petitioners
claim, derive from the possibility that a parent’s child
might run away to a licensed shelter in Washington
and there receive a referral for behavioral health services. After all, children are capable of running away
from one state to another; indeed, it is an issue of such
magnitude that every state in the union has adopted
the Interstate Compact for Juveniles as a means to address it. See, e.g., Wash. Rev. Code § 13.24.011 (recognizing that “each state is responsible for the safe return of juveniles who have run away from home and in
doing so have left their state of residence”). Thus, t he
logic of Petitioners’ theory does not comport with limiting standing  to parents in Washington; it would
seemingly extend so far as to allow Washington’s laws
to be challenged by any parent in the Nation.
Perhaps Petitioners intend for their theory of
standing to be limited to situations where a law purportedly affects parents’ “decisionmaking role as to
gender transitions of their children.” Pet. Br. i; see also
U.S. Amicus Br. 4 (arguing that standing shou ld be
limited to “parents’ control over the medical care their
child may access”). But th e floodgates would be open.
There is far more to the upbringing of children than
decisions about gender transitions and medical care ,
and far more that might conceivab ly induce a child to
buck their parents’ authority or even leave the home—
what Petitioners repeatedly claim is the crux of their
concern. Indeed, “the majority of parent–child conflicts
during adolescence are about typical, everyday family
matters such as home chores, personal hygiene,
friends and social life, and school work.” Anat Moed et
al., Parent–Adolescent Conflict as Sequences of Reciprocal Negative Emotion: Links with Conflict Resolution

13
and Adolescents’ Behavior Problems , 44 J. YOUTH &
ADOLESCENCE 1607, 1608 (2015). The logic of Petitioners’ standing theory would allow any parent to mount
a legal challenge over concerns that a shelter’s policies
with respect to issues such as bedtimes, television
watching, or toothbrushing would conflict with their
own parental approach to those issues. Indeed, on Petitioners’ view, the very existence of shelters available
to adolescent runaways would be subject to challenge
because they could “lure children to run away when
they disagree with their parents.” Pet. Br. 2. So, again,
the logic of Petitioners’ standing theory opens the door
to a wide array of generalized grievances.
Nor does this Court’s emergency order in Mirabelli
v. Bonta, 607 U.S. 492 (2026), save any of the failures
of Petitioners’ standing theory. There, the Court
granted a stay to reinstate a district court’s preliminary injunction against a state policy prohibiting public schools from informing parents that their children
had socially transitioned at school. Id. at 496. In reaching that conclusion, this Court briefly noted that “the
parents protected by the injunction very likely have
standing because they are objects of the challenged exclusion policies.” Id. at 498. The Court also noted that
the “injunction does not provide relief for all the parents of California public school students, but only for
those parents who object to the challenged policies or
seek religious exemptions .” Ibid. Petitioners argue
that this result validates their bid for standing here,
Pet. Br. 26–28, but they are mistaken.
Mirabelli did not—and could not—announce a new
and binding standard for Article III standing. See Merrill v. Milligan, 142 S. Ct. 879, 879 (2022) (Kavanaugh,
J., concurring) (A “stay order is not a decision on the
merits.”). Moreover, even Mirabelli’s preliminary assessment of the standing issue provides no assistance

14
to Petitioners here. This is because Petitioners (and all
other parents in Washington State) are not situated
similarly to the class of parents described as the “objects of the challenged exclusion policies” in Mirabelli.
607 U.S. at 498. That class was limited to parents
whose children were currently subject to the challenged policies in California public schools and who either objected to those policies or sought religious exemptions. Ibid. So, a comparable class for a challenge
to the policies for licensed youth shelters in Washington State at issue here would be  parents whose children are currently in those shelters and who object to
the challenged policies—in other words, a class that by
definition excludes Petitioners and most other parents
in the State.
At the end of the day, if this Court were to “invent
a new doctrine of . . . standing,” as Petitioners propose
to do here, “there would be no principled way to cabin
such a sweeping doctrinal change.”  All. for Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S. at 392 . This Court should “decline to start the Federal Judiciary down that uncharted path.” Texas, 599 U.S. at 681.
C. When coupled with its expansive theory of
parental rights, Petitioners’ novel standing theory threatens to burden important
governmental services—and especially K -
12 public education—with unworkable obligations
Amicus NEA’s primary concern in this case is that,
when Petitioners’ novel theory of standing i s paired
with their expansive theory of parental rights, it will
impose significant and unmanageable burdens on important governmental services, particularly the provision of K -12 education in the Nation’s public schools.
Given the lack of clear limiting principles to Petitioners’ theories, NEA submits that its concerns are well

15
founded and warrant either affirmance of the judgment below or a dismissal of the writ of certiorari as
improvidently granted.
1. At the heart of Petitioners’ claims is the notion
that the Constitution requires near-absolute deference
to each parent’s authority over their child—to the exclusion of the operational needs of a government that
provides services for the entire public. But  this Court
has long been cautious about interpreting constitutional rights in a way that effectively allows “every citizen to become a law unto himself,” reasoning that government “could exist only in name under such circumstances.” Reynolds v. United Sta tes, 98 U.S. 145, 167
(1878); see also Bowen v. Roy , 476 U.S. 693, 699 –700
(1986) (explaining that the Constitution generally does
not require the “Government itself to behave in ways
that the individual believes will further his or her spiritual development or that of his or her family” or “afford an individual a right to dictate the conduct of the
Government's internal procedures”)  (emphasis omitted).
That caution has also extended to claims of parental rights as they relate to the operation of public
schools. See Runyon v. McCrary , 427 U.S. 160, 177
(1976) (rejecting the notion that “parents may replace
state educational requirements with their own idiosyncratic views of what knowledge a child needs to be
a productive and happy member of society”)  (citation
omitted). This is due at least in part to the fact that
the early English (and, before that, Roman) legal tradition—which gave a father an almost absolute right
to the custody, labor, and earnings of his min or children, see 1 William Blackstone, COMMENTARIES *441—
never fully took hold as part of the American legal tradition. For example, Justice Story acknowledged the
earlier common-law rule that a father had an “absolute

16
right to the care and custody of his children” and that
the state lacked the authority to “control the conduct
of the father in the education of his children,” but he
explained that continuing to adhere to such an inflexible rule would now “strike all civilized countries with
astonishment.” Joseph Story, 2 COMMENTARIES ON EQ-
UITY JURISPRUDENCE § 1347 (1836); see also  James
Kent, 2 COMMENTARIES ON AMERICAN LAW 205 (O.W.
Holmes, Jr., ed., 12th ed. 1873)  (explaining that the
code of parent -child relations under Roman law “was
barbarous and unfit for a free and civilized people”);
Lewis Hochheimer, THE LAW RELATING TO THE CUS-
TODY OF INFANTS § 22 (3d ed. 1899)  (explaining that
“the general result of the American cases” is an “utter
repudiation” of the English common-law notion granting parents an absolute “proprietary right of interest
in or to the custody” of children).
Instead, the American tradition of protecting parental rights has been more tempered. See Troxel v.
Granville, 530 U.S. 57, 92 –93 (2000)  (Scalia, J., dissenting) (“[N]o one believes” that “parental rights are
to be absolute.”). And that is especially true when parental prerogatives come into conflict with the operation of public schools. See Morse v. Frederick, 551 U.S.
393, 413–16, 420 (2007) (Thomas, J., concurring) (surveying 19th Century cases that affirm the authority of
schools to “enforce rules” and “maintain order,” including over th e objections of parents). While there were
undoubtedly instances where early American courts
upheld a parent’s request to excuse a child from some
aspect of the school curriculum,4 the majority of cases
from this era recognize that an obligation to conform
to the wishes, values , or preferences of all parents

4 See, e.g., Hardwick v. Bd. of Sch. Trs ., 54 Cal. App. 696
(1921) (excusing child from dancing exercises).
(continued . . .)

17
would be inconsistent with the operational needs of
schools.5 As one of those courts observed:
[T]he power of each parent to decide the question
what studies the scholars should pursue, or what
exercises they should perform, would be a power of
disorganizing the school, and practically rendering
it substantially useless. However judicious it may
be to consult the wishes of parents, the disintegrating principle of parental authority to prevent all
classification and destroy all system in any school,
public or private, is unknown to the law.
Kidder v. Chellis, 59 N.H. 473, 476 (1879).6

Nevertheless, Petitioners advance a conception of
parental rights that puts public institutions at the
mercy of individual preferences, wholly out of step
with this history and tradition. To make matters
worse, they urge a theory of standing that would allow
virtually anyone—including parents whose children

Whereas in Mahmoud v. Taylor, 606 U.S. 522 (2025) ,
the parents were exercising their free exercise right to
control the religious upbringing of their own children,
Petitioners’ theory would establish a seemingly unlimited parental right to control how public institutions
administer programs for all children.
At least as applied to public schools, Petitioners’
position is one that will generate endless administrative confusion, impose burdensome unfunded mandates on schools, and mire federal courts in litigation
over matters far outside their traditional jurisdiction
or expertise. Each of these features  is a sign that
adopting Petitioners’ position would lead this Court,
and the nation’s public schools, down a treacherous
path. See Harris v. Quinn, 573 U.S. 616, 636–37 (2014)
(explaining the dangers of adopting constitutional
rules that will be fraught with “conceptual difficulty”
and “practical administrative problems”).

litigious above all others.
